• Common names: Cajun Dwarf Crayfish, Swamp Dwarf Crayfish, North American Cajun Dwarf Crayfish
  • Optimal tank size: ~40 litres
  • Breeding: easy
  • Optimal KH: 3–15
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: detritivore / omnivore
  • Temperament: conditionally peaceful
  • Life span: up to 2 years
  • Colour: brown/reddish to blue, with two distinct colour patterns (spotted and striped)

Even though Cambarellus shufeldtii is fairly common in North America, these small crayfish are still rather rare in the pet trade. It is easy to breed and care for, does not require frequent water changes or a huge tank, and is one of the most peaceful crayfish species (by crayfish standards). These small animals compensate for their size with personality and plenty of energy.

Cambarellus shufeldtii is easy to feed and care for and is a great choice for beginners. It is full of personality and would make a great addition to a planted tank.

Cambarellus shufeldtii is a freshwater crayfish of the family Cambaridae, native to the Gulf Coastal Plain of the United States, which includes the states of Alabama, Arkansas, Illinois, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Tennessee and Texas. It has a large distribution and can inhabit a wide range of habitats; for example, it is present in Georgia as an introduced species.

In nature, Cambarellus shufeldtii prefers shallow habitats with standing to slow-moving water, including swamps, marshes, lakes, ponds, ditches, sluggish streams and slow rivers. It favours shallow water with plant cover.

The number of crayfish determines the tank size. For example, 5–10 adults can be kept in a 40-litre tank with lots of cover. One adult in an 8-litre tank is technically possible but not practical: they are active and need plenty of room to crawl, eat and explore, and in small tanks everything can go wrong very fast. The smallest recommended size is 20 litres. If you plan to breed them, go bigger to give the offspring more space.

These crayfish are excellent escape artists and can spend some time out of the water, so use a lid and make sure the water level is not too high.

If you are a first-time crayfish owner, cycle the tank before bringing any crayfish home, then check water quality with a test kit. Although they are low-maintenance and easy to care for, always try to replicate their natural environment as closely as possible. It is better to acclimate them as well.

Cambarellus shufeldtii is safe with any live plants. Because of its small size there is little danger: it does not dig up plants (as larger crayfish do) and does not eat healthy plants, so it can be kept in beautifully planted aquariums.

Molting is how it grows, and it also allows lost limbs to be restored. The crayfish sheds its exoskeleton and for a short time afterwards cannot move until it regains muscle control and the new exoskeleton hardens. Before molting it looks for a place to hide; otherwise it can easily fall prey to tankmates.

  • Never disturb crayfish while they molt. Do not panic if you do not see them for a few days.
  • Keep putting in and replacing food.
  • Keep giving calcium-rich food.
  • Do not remove the old exoskeleton from the tank; it contains lots of minerals and the crayfish will eat it later.

Temperature: they tolerate a wide range of 18–26 °C, but the optimal range in the aquarium is 20–24 °C. They do not need a heater; room temperature suits them fine.

pH: according to the study, they can tolerate a pH range of at least 5.4–7.4.

Hardness: optimal KH 3–15 and GH 3–18.

Filtration: given the tank size, sponge filters are the simplest option (cheap and effective). They do not tear apart the sponge as large crayfish often do, except when lots of gunk has accumulated in it and they chew the sponge to get at it. Any filter can be used as long as young cannot be sucked in; if you use a canister or hang-on-back filter and plan to breed them, cover the intake with a sponge or net.

Lighting: they prefer subdued lighting, but in planted tanks lighting should be adapted to the plants.

Substrate: soil and/or sand substrates are ideal.

Decorations: provide lots of hiding places, at least 2 per crayfish. Live or artificial plants, leaves, rocks, driftwood, PVC pipes, bricks, cones and so on all work. They also like spots as narrow as possible for them to fit in. Tip: use large items (such as big rocks) throughout the tank so they are less likely to bump into one another. This is also crucial for molting, as cannibalism after molting can become a problem.

Cambarellus shufeldtii are natural scavengers: omnivores and opportunistic eaters that will eat almost anything they find. In captivity, for best growth they need a good mix of meat, vegetation and calcium, with protein at about 30–40% of the diet.

Foods they enjoy:

  • Shrimp pellets and granules
  • Fish food (e.g. flakes)
  • Shrimp food (crustacean foods such as Hikari Shrimp Cuisine)
  • Vegetables (broccoli, cabbage, carrot, cucumber, lettuce, corn, spinach, peas, squash, leafy greens, etc.)
  • Fruits (apple, banana, pear, melon, mango, etc.)
  • Leaves
  • Frozen bloodworms
  • Detritus worms
  • Brine shrimp
  • Tubifex worms
  • Blackworms
  • Earthworms
  • Freshly crushed snails
  • Dead fish or shrimp, etc.

Leaves (for example Indian almond leaves, dead beech or oak leaves) should always be on the menu, as they feed on these and on the detritus from the leaves. Supplement the diet with eggshells, cuttlebone and so on, and make sure they get enough calcium for the exoskeleton by regularly feeding specialised invertebrate foods.

They can be awkward during feeding; for example, tubifex worms can get away faster than they can find them.

Adults can be fed 3–4 times a week, while juveniles should be fed daily. Food can be left for 24 hours before removal; leaves can stay in the tank for days or weeks. It is better to feed them at night (at least in the evening), as they are nocturnal. Adjust to your livestock's needs: crayfish are scavengers, so they also get a share when tankmates are fed. Do not let them starve, or they may go after shrimp and fry, or even cannibalise each other.

Without large or aggressive fish, they are active and not timid at all. They are often seen crawling around the tank day and night, but are still considered nocturnal. They are outgoing and far more social than other species. Unlike dwarf Mexican crayfish, which will not tolerate another male in sight, they are generally much easier. They may spar at times (mostly over food) but usually do not cause damage and prefer to retreat.

In nature they can burrow during dry periods, but they are not obligate burrowers; given a chance they mostly occupy existing burrows and hollow them out. They are not messy or destructive and will not redecorate the aquascape.

  • Social: yes
  • Active: yes
  • Peaceful: yes (generally)
  • Burrowers: no (generally)

Tankmates: generally safe with plants, fish and shrimp, but opportunistic, so they may occasionally go after a tankmate because of underfeeding, improper diet, overstocking or individual temper.

Fish: do not keep with aggressive, bottom-dwelling, slow-moving or long-finned fish (such as bettas). They cannot kill most fish but may damage fins at night. They are often kept with small peaceful fish such as guppies, neon tetras, mollies, Endler's livebearers and dwarf swordtails.

Shrimp: there are many reports of them kept in shrimp tanks without losses, but even if chasing is not noticed they regularly snap at shrimp that come too close, and many shrimp lose antennae; the accumulated harassment stresses shrimp. Keeping them with expensive shrimp is risky, especially when shrimp molt. If kept together, keep the crayfish well fed and provide enough hiding places for both.

Snails: they usually do not bother big snails, though they may nip off antennae; baby snails can end up as a snack.

Bad tankmates: larger or aggressive fish; bottom-dwelling, slow-moving and long-finned fish; any other crayfish species; other freshwater crabs; dwarf frogs.

Cambarellus shufeldtii is sexually dimorphic.

  • Abdomen: the sexes can be told apart by the lower part of the abdomen. Males have an extra set of pleopods used for internal fertilisation, seen as a triangular-ish formation of small legs, and their first pleopods are more rigid. Females have a seminal receptacle and lack the extra pleopods behind the walking legs, showing only a small nub. Females have a wider abdomen.
  • Size: females are a little larger, usually reaching about 33 mm total body length, while males generally range between 15 and 30 mm.
  • Claws: female pincers are shorter and thicker; males have relatively slender and long pincers.

Cambarellus shufeldtii is very prolific and breeds readily. Young grow rapidly and mature after about 2 months at roughly 18 mm total length. An average female produces at least 2 broods in her lifetime.

A receptive female allows a male to approach; he then clamps her claws and puts her on her back. Mating can last from several minutes to an hour or so.

According to the study, female reproductive traits correlate positively with body size, number of eggs and number of juveniles. Females usually carry 15–74 eggs (average 45). They use their appendages to keep the eggs clean and well oxygenated, yet mortality is high (up to 44%) in egg and early juvenile stages.

Hatching usually takes 3–4 weeks depending on temperature. Newly hatched young are a little bigger than baby cherry shrimp (about 3 mm) and grow faster. They stay with the mother for about 7–10 days. Females usually do not attack their babies, but ideally they should be isolated in a separate rearing tank. Babies can be fed the same food as adults in smaller portions; there is little cannibalism if they are not overcrowded.

Cambarellus shufeldtii can grow up to about 3.5 cm; the average size is around 3 cm, with females slightly larger. The claws are narrow and long. Colour patterns are variable, which makes them hard to identify: some individuals are brown, some more reddish, some light tan with reddish claws. The background colour can be tan to light brown, and some may have longitudinal dark stripes on the carapace and abdomen. Like many crustaceans, young show little colour.

Blue strains also exist. According to the study, they can show two bluish patterns, with no intermediate or blending between them:

  • A spotted form, with several rows of dark steel-blue spots on the dorso-lateral surfaces of the carapace and abdomen.
  • A striped form, with several rows of dark steel-blue stripes alternating with pigmentless stripes of equal width along the carapace and abdomen.

Colour is variable and changes as they grow and molt. Some keepers are still trying to create a pure blue strain, but these crayfish do not yet breed true.

Lifespan: they live rather short lives of no more than 15–18 months (up to 2 years in captivity under optimal conditions). According to some studies, females live about 1 year, during which they may have at least two broods. Lifespan is probably limited by physical exhaustion due to the high energy cost of breeding in species with direct development. In a poorly maintained aquarium they can suffer and die prematurely.

Other dwarf species: the genus is reported to contain 19 species, all small and similar, so telling them apart is almost impossible for non-specialists. Colour is sometimes used (C. ninae brown; C. montezumae yellow; C. patzcuarensis orange; C. shufeldtii grey/reddish to brown; C. texanus olive to brown; C. diminutus grey/reddish to dark grey; C. puer orange-red to light brown), but this is not accurate because colour varies within a species and is affected by diet and selection. Many Cambarellus species also hybridise in the wild, creating new colour variations, and some aquarists use this to create new colour morphs.
